notes.meaning: God gives instructions for a peace offering using cattle, allowing either a male or female animal as long as it has no flaws. This sacrifice was brought to celebrate friendship and harmony with the Lord, often to say thank you or ask for a blessing. A whole burnt offering required a male because it focused on atonement—making things right between God and sinners—but here either sex was accepted because the meal celebrated peaceful communion with God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching sees the peace offering as a picture of the Mass, where Christ offers Himself so believers can share in the sacrificial meal of peace.

notes.meaning: The worshiper presses his hand onto the animal's head and slaughters it at the entrance of the sacred tent, while the priests splash its blood against the sides of the altar. Placing a hand on the creature showed that the worshiper was dedicating this gift to God with praise. Even in a joyful meal of friendship, the shed blood reminded the people that peace with God always rests on a life given in sacrifice.

The worshiper takes out the best internal fat that covers and clings to the intestines, along with both kidneys and a part of the liver. To the ancient Israelites, the kidneys and liver stood for a person's deepest feelings, thoughts, and inner vitality. Fat was considered the richest part of the meat, so burning it showed that God deserves the very best of a person's strength and devotion.

The priests place these fatty parts on the altar on top of the daily morning burnt offering. The burnt offering dealt with sin first, which showed that peaceful fellowship with God can only happen after forgiveness is secured. As the fat burned, the smoke rose as a pleasing aroma, showing that God warmly received their worship.

God explains that a worshiper can also bring a sheep or a goat from the flock, whether male or female, as long as it has no defects. Sheep and goats were less expensive than cattle, which allowed ordinary families to share in this offering of fellowship. Just like cattle, the animal had to be healthy and whole because God always deserves an unblemished gift.

When a person brings a lamb, he presents it before the Lord, rests his hand on its head, and slaughters it in front of the tent before the priests splash the blood around the altar. The steps followed the exact same pattern of personal dedication and blood sacrifice as an offering of cattle. The gentle surrender of the lamb reminded the worshiper to come before God with a humble, grateful heart.

From the lamb, the worshiper removes the kidneys, liver lobe, internal fat, and the entire fat tail sliced off close to the backbone. Middle Eastern sheep had wide tails packed with rich fat, which people considered a prized delicacy for feasts. Instead of keeping that choice treat for his own family, the worshiper gave it completely to the Lord on the altar fire.

The priest burns all these parts on the altar fire as food for the Lord. Calling this gift God's food did not mean the Lord needed to eat, unlike the false gods of nearby nations. It was a word picture showing that God was sharing a meal at the same table with His people and delighting in their friendship.

If the worshiper chooses a goat, he brings it before the Lord, lays his hand on its head, slaughters it, and the priests sprinkle its blood against the altar. Goats were listed separately from sheep because they do not have broad, fatty tails, but the rest of the sacred ceremony was identical. God welcomed this offering just as freely, opening the way for anyone to come near and rejoice in His presence.

The worshiper separates the inner fat covering the organs, the fat attached to them, the two kidneys, and the lobe of the liver from the goat. Just as with the bull and the sheep, the richest inner portions were taken out for the Lord. Presenting these hidden parts served as a reminder to give God one's whole heart and deepest loyalty.

The priest burns these parts on the altar as food, producing a sweet aroma that pleases the Lord, and God announces that all the fat belongs to Him. Fire consumed the richest portions as God's special share of the meal before the priest and worshiper ate the rest. Because fat represented the best and most valuable part of the animal, it was reserved for God alone.

God sets down a lasting law for all generations, commanding the Israelites never to eat any fat or any blood, no matter where they live. The fat was God's sacred share on the altar, and the blood carried the life of the animal used to make atonement for human souls. This rule trained the people to practice self-control and honor God's holy claims in their everyday meals.

differ.view: The permanent rule against eating blood was tied to the Old Testament sacrificial system and ended when Christ shed his blood on the cross.
Christians should still avoid consuming blood because the apostles in Acts 15 repeated this command for the church.
